problem.heading: DMARC holds the evidence — in a format built for machines.
problem.sub: The reports that could tell you who sends as you, and whether they authenticate, arrive as raw XML. Almost nobody reads them, so three things quietly go wrong.

cards.title: You don't know who sends as you
cards.body: Spoofing runs silent, and so does the form tool, the CRM or the agency nobody told you about. Every one of them is already in your reports, with its IP and its volume.

cards.title: Legitimate mail quietly fails
cards.body: A missing SPF include or a revoked DKIM key sends your real mail to spam. Since 2024 Google and Yahoo also require DMARC from anyone sending over 5,000 messages a day to their users.

cards.title: You never reach enforcement
cards.body: Staying at p=none feels safe, but it leaves the door open. Moving to reject without knowing every legitimate sender is a gamble — so most domains never move.

features.heading: A verdict, not a data dump.
features.sub: Sentinely turns raw aggregate reports into decisions: a score to track, sources you can name, records you can fix, changes you'd otherwise miss, and alerts that reach you before anyone else notices.

cards.title: Deliverability & protection score
cards.body: A 0–100 score with an A–F grade per domain, built from authentication, policy, hygiene and blocklist status — with a confidence indicator while the data is still thin.

cards.title: Every sending source, named
cards.body: IP, hostname (rDNS/PTR), geolocation and organisation/ASN for each source, plus a clear line between senders you've seen before and ones that have never sent for you.

cards.title: Records read, not just found
cards.body: SPF, DKIM, DMARC, BIMI, MTA-STS and TLS-RPT checked for how they're written: fused DMARC tags, rua without mailto:, unknown SPF mechanisms, the 10-lookup limit. With the exact record to publish.

cards.title: The changes, not only the current state
cards.body: Every analysis run compares your DNS with the previous observation and records what moved — the value before, the value after, and when. A DMARC policy walked back to p=none, an SPF include that disappeared, an MX pointing somewhere new: each one raises an alert.

cards.title: DKIM selectors, found in your reports
cards.body: DNS offers no way to list a domain's DKIM selectors, so most tools leave you typing them from memory. Sentinely collects the ones that appear in your DMARC reports and proposes them; you confirm yours with a click. Partial by construction — many senders omit the selector — and far better than a blank field.

cards.title: How much your SPF actually authorises
cards.body: The number of IPv4 addresses your record lets send as you, next to how many of them did in the last 90 days. The quickest way to see the surface a forgotten include leaves open — and a floor, not a total, since it counts the addresses written literally in the record.

cards.title: Reputation & blocklist watch
cards.body: Continuous DNSBL/RBL checks on the IPs sending for your domain, with a three-state result — listed, clean, or not checkable — so uncertainty never reads as safety.

cards.title: Alerts, and one digest for everything
cards.body: A new source, a volume anomaly against the 7-day average, a high failure rate, mail quarantined or rejected, a record that changed. Plus one digest per person — every domain you watch in a single email, worst first — daily, weekly or both, in each recipient's language.

cards.title: Multi-tenant, white-label, API
cards.body: A separate space per client with per-domain access, your name, colour, logo and footer on the app, emails and PDFs, and a read-only REST API with a per-tenant key.

how.heading: One record in. Control out.
how.sub: No agents, no gateway changes, no mail rerouting. You publish a single DMARC record and Sentinely does the reading.

steps.title: Publish your RUA
steps.body: Add one DMARC record pointing aggregate reports at a Sentinely address. That's the only change on your side — or push the reports yourself over a signed HTTP webhook.

steps.title: We ingest & identify
steps.body: XML, GZIP and ZIP parsed and de-duplicated. Every source resolved to an IP, host, location and organisation, then checked for authentication, alignment and blocklist status. Each run also compares your DNS with the previous observation, so a changed record doesn't pass unnoticed.

steps.title: Read the verdict, act
steps.body: Fix what's weak with the record we hand you, keep your campaigns authenticated, and move from p=none to enforcement with the data to back the decision.

changes.heading: A record is right until someone edits it.
changes.sub: The configuration you set up rarely stays as you left it: a client, a technician or the registrar changes something, and nobody notices. Every analysis run compares your DNS with the previous observation and records the difference — the value before, the value after, the day it moved.

points.title: MX and NS, not only the auth records
points.body: Where your mail is delivered, and who controls your zone. An MX that moves from Microsoft 365 to an unknown host either breaks your incoming mail or means someone reached your DNS — so both records are tracked and land in the same timeline. Neither touches your score: this is monitoring, not a grade.

points.title: DKIM selectors you never had to type
points.body: DNS gives no way to list the selectors published for a domain, so anyone who doesn't already know them is analysing blind. Sentinely collects the selectors that appear in your DMARC reports and proposes them; you confirm yours with a click. The inventory is partial — plenty of senders leave the selector out — and we'd rather say so than call it complete.

points.title: How wide your SPF is open
points.body: One line tells you how many addresses your record authorises to send as you, and how many of them actually did. The gap is the surface a forgotten include leaves behind — and you don't need to know what SPF is to read it.

points.title: History starts the day you do
points.body: No DNS query can recover what a record said last month, and we won't pretend otherwise. The timeline begins when the domain is added; from that point on, nothing changes without being written down.

items.q: Do I need to be a DMARC expert?
items.a: No. Sentinely translates raw aggregate reports into plain-language verdicts and tells you exactly which record to publish. If you can edit a DNS entry, you're set.

items.q: Will it change my email or my DNS?
items.a: No. Sentinely only receives the DMARC reports you route to it. It never publishes or edits your DNS records: it works out the exact record you need and shows it to you — publishing stays with you.

items.q: What's the difference between Free and the trial?
items.a: They are two separate plans, and both cost nothing. Free is perpetual: one domain, one user, 1,000 messages a month, 30 days of history, no end date. Trial is a plan in its own right lasting 30 days — three domains, three users, 10,000 messages a month, with every feature and add-on switched on, AI Insights and white-label included. Neither asks for a card. When the trial's 30 days are up you move to Free automatically; nothing is locked and your data stays readable.

items.q: How quickly will I see results?
items.a: As soon as your RUA points at us, reports start flowing. Mailbox providers send aggregate reports roughly once a day, so most domains get their first full verdict and digest within 24 hours.

items.q: Do you tell me when my DNS changes?
items.a: Yes — from the day you add the domain. Every analysis run compares your DNS with the previous observation and records the difference: the value before, the value after, when it moved, with an alert. That covers SPF, DKIM, DMARC, BIMI, MTA-STS and TLS-RPT, and also MX and NS — where your mail is delivered and who controls your zone — though those two are monitoring only and don't affect the score. What we can't do is reconstruct the past: no DNS query can tell you what a record said last month, so the timeline starts when the monitoring does.

items.q: Do I need to know my DKIM selectors?
items.a: It helps, but no. DNS provides no way to list the selectors published for a domain, so if you don't know them there's nowhere to look them up. Sentinely collects the selectors that appear in your DMARC reports and proposes them; you confirm the ones that are yours with a click. The inventory is partial by construction — many systems that send reports omit the selector — so you can still add by hand any you know about.
No — aggregate reports only. That means Sentinely never holds copies of individual messages: it works from the counts, sources and authentication results that providers report in aggregate.

items.q: Can I manage multiple domains and clients?
items.a: Yes. Sentinely has been multi-tenant since day one: separate spaces per client, per-domain access assignable to individual users, white-label branding across the app, emails and PDFs, and a read-only REST API with a per-tenant key.

It isn't a mail gateway — it doesn't route, filter or block mail, and it doesn't replace your SEG or anti-spam. It doesn't do inbox-placement testing, seed lists or spam-trap monitoring, and it doesn't validate BIMI VMC certificates. There's no SSO/SAML, and white-label doesn't put the application on your own domain. The score reads the DMARC data you receive — it isn't a guarantee of inbox delivery.

items.q: Where is my data stored, and in which languages do you work?
items.a: DMARC report data is processed and stored in the EU and retained on a rolling window — see our GDPR/DPA page for the specifics. The interface, alerts, daily digest and AI Insights are all available in both English and Italian.

problem.heading: Sending volume isn't the hard part. Not knowing is.

cards.title: Google and Yahoo already require it

cards.title: Senders you never approved
cards.body: A form tool here, a CRM there, an agency that kept sending after the contract ended. Each one appears in your aggregate reports with its IP, its host and its volume.

cards.title: You changed platform and something broke
cards.body: A migration that missed a DKIM selector or an SPF include fails quietly. Engagement tells you weeks later; the aggregate reports tell you the next morning.

cards.title: A deliverability score to track

cards.title: A change you didn't make
cards.body: A migration that drops an SPF include, a policy someone walks back, an MX repointed by the registrar. Each analysis run compares your DNS with the previous observation and tells you what moved, with the value before and the value after.

cards.title: DKIM selectors, without asking your ESP
cards.body: DNS won't list the selectors published for a domain, so most tools ask you to type them. Sentinely picks up the ones that appear in your DMARC reports and proposes them for confirmation — partial, since many senders omit the selector, but usually enough to stop guessing.

cards.title: How many senders your SPF allows
cards.body: Every platform you have ever added leaves an include behind. Sentinely counts the IPv4 addresses your record authorises and how many of them sent in the last 90 days — the gap is what you can safely clean up. Read the count as a floor: it covers the addresses written literally in the record.

cards.title: Blocklist watch on your senders
cards.body: Continuous DNSBL/RBL checks on the IPs sending for your domain, with a three-state result so 'not checkable' never gets read as 'clean'.

cards.title: The record to publish, written out
cards.body: An SPF record past the 10-lookup limit, a DMARC tag fused to the next by a missing semicolon, a revoked DKIM key. Sentinely finds it and hands you the exact record.

It reads the aggregate reports providers send about your domain — which is where sender identity, authentication and policy live. Placement testing is a different instrument; this one tells you whether your mail is authenticated and who is sending it.

meta.title: DMARC monitoring for IT & Sec Ops — Sentinely
meta.description: Name every source sending as your domain, read your SPF, DKIM, DMARC, BIMI, MTA-STS and TLS-RPT records for real syntax errors, get an alert when one of them changes, and move from p=none to p=reject without blocking legitimate mail.

security.title: Stop impersonation. Reach p=reject with the data to prove it's safe.
security.sub: The evidence you need to enforce DMARC already arrives every day, as XML nobody reads. Sentinely reads it, names every sender, and shows you what would break before you change the policy.

problem.heading: Staying at p=none is a decision too.
problem.sub: It's the decision to leave your domain usable by anyone, and to find out about it from whoever got the phish.

cards.title: Anyone can send as you
cards.body: Until DMARC is enforced your domain is a free identity. Phishing sent from it arrives with your name on it, and the first you hear of it is from the person who received it.

cards.title: Enforcement without data is a gamble
cards.body: Move to p=reject before you know every legitimate sender and you'll block your own invoices, tickets or payroll mail. Which is why most domains never move.

cards.title: Broken auth hides in plain sight
cards.body: A revoked DKIM key, an SPF record past the 10-lookup ceiling, terms placed after "all" that will never be evaluated. Published, present, and silently failing.

value.heading: Enough evidence to change the policy.
value.sub: Read-only, from the aggregate reports your domain already receives. Nothing to install, nothing in the mail path.

cards.title: Every source resolved
cards.body: IP, hostname (rDNS/PTR), geolocation and organisation/ASN for each sender, plus a clear line between sources you already know and ones that have never sent for your domain.

cards.title: Records read for syntax
cards.body: SPF, DKIM, DMARC, BIMI, MTA-STS and TLS-RPT checked for how they're written: fused DMARC tags, rua or ruf without mailto:, invalid sp and pct, unknown SPF mechanisms, invalid ip4/ip6, deprecated ptr, the 10-lookup limit.

cards.title: Changes recorded, with before and after
cards.body: Each run compares your DNS with the previous observation and records the difference — value before, value after, when. A policy walked back to p=none, an SPF include gone, a BIMI record removed. MX and NS are watched the same way, though neither touches the score.

cards.title: DKIM selectors, discovered
cards.body: DNS can't be asked to list the selectors published for a domain, so most tools leave you a blank field. Sentinely harvests the selectors that appear in your aggregate reports and proposes them for confirmation. Partial by nature — many senders omit the selector — but it turns a blind analysis into a working one.

cards.title: The size of what your SPF authorises
cards.body: The count of IPv4 addresses your record permits, next to how many of them sent in the last 90 days. A forgotten include can authorise hundreds of thousands of hosts while a handful do the sending. The count covers the addresses written literally in the record, so treat it as a floor.

cards.title: A protection score with a grade
cards.body: 0–100 and A–F across authentication, policy, hygiene and blocklist status, with a confidence indicator while there isn't yet enough data to be sure.

cards.title: Alerts with a severity threshold
cards.body: New source never seen before, volume anomaly against the 7-day average, high failure rate, mail quarantined or rejected from a known source. Configurable per recipient and per domain.

cards.title: Blocklist monitoring
cards.body: Continuous DNSBL/RBL checks on every IP sending for the domain, with a three-state result — listed, clean, or not checkable.

cards.title: A warning when reports stop
cards.body: A domain that suddenly stops receiving aggregate reports usually means a broken configuration, not quiet skies. Sentinely tells you instead of letting the silence look like success.

note.heading: What this is not
note.body: Sentinely doesn't route, filter or block mail — it isn't a gateway and it doesn't replace your SEG or anti-spam. It ingests aggregate (RUA) reports only, never forensic/RUF, so there are no copies of individual messages anywhere in it. It doesn't validate BIMI VMC certificates, and it offers no SSO/SAML. It never publishes or edits your DNS: it computes the record and shows it to you, and publishing stays with you.

about.heading: Email authentication, made legible.
about.sub: Sentinely exists because the evidence already arrives every day — trapped in XML nobody reads. We turn it into something a person can act on.

sections.heading: What we do
sections.body: You publish a single DNS record. From then on, mailbox providers worldwide send us the DMARC aggregate reports for your domain. We parse them, resolve every sending source, check authentication, alignment, record syntax and blocklist status, compare your DNS with the previous observation to catch what changed, and return a verdict: a 0–100 score with a grade, alerts, a digest and reports you can export.

sections.heading: Who it's for
sections.body: Marketing teams who need their campaigns to authenticate and to know which platforms send in their name. IT and security teams taking a domain from p=none to enforcement. And the agencies, MSPs and consultants who do both, for many clients at once — multi-tenant, white-label, with a read-only API.

sections.heading: How we talk about it
sections.body: Sentinely reads aggregate reports. It is not a mail gateway, it does not test inbox placement, and it never touches your DNS. We would rather tell you what it doesn't do than have you find out later — so the limits are written down next to the features, on every page.

headerAnalyzer.title: Email header analyzer
headerAnalyzer.sub: Paste the headers of an email and read what they actually say: what the receiving server reported for SPF, DKIM and DMARC, whether the visible sender matches the domain that authenticated, the route the message took and where it lost time.

form.label: Paste the email headers
form.hint: The whole message is fine — everything after the first blank line is the body, and your browser drops it before sending.
form.helpLink: Where do I find the headers?

privacy.title: Nothing you paste is stored
privacy.body: Email headers are other people's personal data — senders, recipients, IP addresses, subject lines — and the people named in them never agreed to anything. So your browser sends them straight to our analysis API, which reads them and forgets them: nothing is written to a database, a file or a log. This page keeps nothing either — no history, no browser storage, and not one character of what you paste reaches any analytics tool. Close the tab and it's gone.

errors.tooLarge: That's more than the analyser accepts ({size}, limit {max}). Paste only the header block — from the first line down to the first blank line.
errors.rateLimited: That's several analyses in a short time. Wait a minute and try again — the limit is what keeps the tool open to everyone without a sign-up.
errors.unprocessable: These headers couldn't be read. Check that you pasted the block whole, from the first line down to the first blank line.
errors.network: The analyser couldn't be reached. Check your connection and try again.
errors.server: The analyser didn't answer as expected. Try again in a moment.

unrecognized.title: No headers found in that text
unrecognized.body: Nothing in what you pasted looks like an email header — this is the usual first try. Headers are the technical lines above the message, each one starting with a name and a colon: Received:, From:, Authentication-Results:. Your mail client hides them by default; the steps below show how to reveal them in the one you use.

result.reportedByUnknown: The receiving server did not name itself

auth.heading: What the receiving server reported
auth.sub: These lines were written by the server that received the message. Sentinely reads them — it does not re-run the checks, and it could not: the headers you pasted are the only evidence here.
auth.absentTitle: These headers carry no authentication results
auth.absentBody: That is not a failure — it means nothing was reported, so nothing can be said about SPF, DKIM or DMARC. It is normal for a copy taken from the Sent folder, and for a paste that stops before the receiving server had its say.

arc.label: ARC
arc.hint: ARC carries the original results across a forwarder or a mailing list.

alignment.heading: Does the visible sender match?
alignment.sub: This is what DMARC actually asks: the domain your reader sees in the From line has to match the domain that authenticated. A message can pass SPF and still fail DMARC, because it passed for somebody else’s domain.
alignment.approximated: One domain is a subdomain of the other, which satisfies DMARC’s default (relaxed) alignment. Confirming the organisational domain exactly would need the public suffix list, which is deliberately not consulted here — nothing you paste triggers a lookup.
alignment.noFromDomain: These headers carry no visible From address, so there is nothing to align against.

path.heading: The route it took
path.sub: Every server that handled the message stamped a line on the way. Read top to bottom — oldest first, with the time each step took.
path.clockSkew: At least one server’s clock disagrees with the one before it, so some steps cannot be timed. The timestamps below are read exactly as written.
path.timezone: Timestamps are shown in your own time zone.
path.empty: These headers carry no Received lines, so there is no route to show.

limits.heading: Not all of the input was analysed
limits.headersTruncated: The message carried more headers than the analyser reads; the extra ones were ignored.
limits.hopsTruncated: The message carried more Received lines than the analyser reads; the oldest were dropped.
limits.valuesTruncated: At least one header was too long and was cut before being read.

find.heading: Where the headers hide, client by client
find.sub: Every mail client keeps them one menu away from the message. Copy everything you see — the block is long, and the useful lines are usually at the top.

clients.name: Gmail (web)
clients.steps: Open the message, click the ⋮ menu at the top right of the message itself (not the one in the toolbar) and choose “Show original”. The page that opens has a “Copy to clipboard” button — it copies the whole message, which is fine.

clients.name: Outlook (Windows, desktop)
clients.steps: Open the message in its own window, then File → Properties. The headers are in the “Internet headers” box at the bottom: click inside it, select all, copy.

clients.name: Outlook on the web / Outlook.com
clients.steps: Open the message, click the ⋯ menu at the top right and choose “View” → “View message details”. Copy everything in the panel.

clients.name: Apple Mail (macOS)
clients.steps: Select the message, then View → Message → All Headers (⇧⌘H). For the complete block use View → Message → Raw Source (⌥⌘U) and copy from the top down to the first blank line.

clients.name: Thunderbird
clients.steps: Select the message and press Ctrl+U (⌘U on macOS) for the source, or View → Headers → All to see them inline.

clients.name: Yahoo Mail
clients.steps: Open the message, click the ⋯ (More) menu and choose “View raw message”. Copy the whole page.

find.note: Forwarding the email to yourself does not work: forwarding writes a fresh set of headers and buries the original ones in the body. Use “Show original” or “Raw source” on the message you actually received.

read.heading: What the answer tells you — and what it cannot

cards.title: The results are claims, not checks
cards.body: SPF, DKIM and DMARC results sit in the headers because the receiving server wrote them there when the message arrived. Reading them tells you what that server concluded at that moment. Nobody can re-run the check afterwards: the message has already been delivered, and DNS may have changed since.

cards.title: Missing is not failing
cards.body: Headers with no authentication results have not failed authentication — nothing was reported. A copy from your Sent folder has none, and neither does a paste that stops too early. Read silence as “unknown”, never as “bad”.

cards.title: Alignment is the part that bites
cards.body: SPF can pass for the platform that sent the message while the address your reader sees is yours. DMARC only accepts a pass whose domain matches the visible From — which is why a message can pass SPF and still be rejected.

cards.title: The delays are real, the clocks may not be
cards.body: Each Received line carries the time its server stamped. Add them up and you can see where a message waited. But those clocks belong to different organisations: when one disagrees with the one before it, that step is flagged rather than guessed.

cards.title: One message is one message
cards.body: A header block describes a single delivery to a single recipient. It cannot tell you how much mail leaves your domain, who else sends as you, or whether yesterday’s campaign authenticated — that lives in the aggregate reports mailbox providers already send about your domain.

cards.title: Nothing here is looked up
cards.body: The analysis reads the text you paste and nothing else: no DNS query, no connection to any server named in the headers, no signature verification. That is what keeps it fast and private, and it is also the limit — a domain written in a header is a claim like everything else.

items.q: Do you store the headers I paste?
items.a: No. They go from your browser to the analysis API, which reads them and returns the result without writing them to a database, a file or a log. The page keeps nothing either: no history, no browser storage, nothing sent to analytics. Reload and it is gone.
No. No sign-up, no email address to leave, no limit per person — just a cap of a few analyses per minute, so the tool stays open to everyone.

items.q: Can I paste the whole email, body and all?
items.a: Yes. Everything after the first blank line is the body: your browser drops it before sending, so only the header block ever leaves your machine. If the block itself is enormous, the tool says so before sending anything.

items.q: It says “no headers found” — what did I do wrong?
items.a: Almost always the message was forwarded instead of exported. Forwarding writes fresh headers and buries the originals in the body. Go back to the message you received and use “Show original” (Gmail), “Properties” (Outlook) or “Raw source” (Apple Mail).

items.q: SPF says pass but DMARC says fail. How?
items.a: Because they look at different domains. SPF checks the envelope sender, which usually belongs to the platform that sent the message. DMARC only counts a pass whose domain matches the From address your reader sees. When the two differ and DKIM does not cover it either, DMARC fails.

items.q: Does this tell me whether my domain is protected?
items.a: No — it reads one message. What leaves your domain every day, who else sends in your name and whether that mail authenticates lives in the DMARC aggregate reports mailbox providers already send about your domain. That is what Sentinely does the rest of the time.

cta.heading: That was one message. What about all the others?
cta.sub: Mailbox providers already report on every message sent in your name. Publish one DNS record and Sentinely turns those reports into the same kind of plain answer — for the whole domain, every day.
